extracted.intended_audience: general English‑speaking newspaper readers / wartime public
extracted.subtask_description: News reporting focused on aerial raids and their effects: factual chronologies of attacks, official communiqués, casualty/damage counts, defense actions, and human-interest details to convey impact and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include official communique summaries
rubrics_metrics.description: Use and quote official ministry communiqués (Air Ministry, Home Securities Ministries) to summarize the day's raids, areas attacked, and official assessments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language from page: “Throughout this morning individual enemy aircraft kept up a series of attacks … The casualties both in London and elsewhere were very slight.” The article repeatedly cites formal communiqués to present authoritative, consolidated information on attacks, targets and immediate official judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report casualty and damage counts (with totals and updates)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide specific numbers of dead, injured and damaged properties and update running totals where available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example language: “Wednesday night’s raids killed 110 … bringing the totals from last Saturday through Wednesday to 1,245 dead and 4,810 injured.” Include counts for particular raids/towns and aggregate figures when provided by officials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a precise chronological timeline (alarms, times, durations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Give times of alarms, start/end of raids, durations and sequence of events to situate the reader in the unfolding incident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story records many times: “signal came at 3.27 A. M. … The all-clear sounded at 5.05 P. M. … the fourth alarm ended at 7.13 P. M.” Include durations (e.g., 2-hour-and-11-minute alarm) and sequence of successive alarms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Describe defensive actions and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Report military and civil defenses (RAF sorties, anti-aircraft barrages, searchlights) and outcomes such as enemy planes shot down or lost own aircraft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “Up to 8.30 P. M., the Air Ministry announced, eleven German planes had been shot down … The Royal Air Force … attacked enemy shipping … Concentrations of barges were wrecked.” Note both defensive activity and its reported effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide strategic/military context and analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain larger tactical or strategic significance (tests of defenses, invasion danger, changes in enemy tactics) to help readers understand implications beyond immediate damage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Phrases used: “The next forty‑eight hours ‘is a period of intense danger of invasion’ … The three daylight attacks seemed to be intended principally to feel out the state of the English coastal defenses … constituted a departure from the week‑long German tactics.” Present analysts’ or neutral military sources’ assessments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include eyewitness, correspondent and official quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate on‑the‑ground correspondent reports, witness accounts and spokesmen’s statements to add authority and immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: “A correspondent at Deal, on the southeast coast, said …” and quoted spokesmen in Berlin; use direct speech or attributed paraphrase from officials, correspondents and neutral sources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance factual reporting with human-interest details
rubrics_metrics.description: Augment the factual account with human‑interest elements (civilian casualties, refugees, anecdotes, morale) to convey the human impact of events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece includes: deaths in a church crypt, refugees demanding shelter at the Savoy, Boy Scout bagpipe band anecdote, and repair crews—use such items to illustrate civilian experience and morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report damage to landmarks and cultural sites
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and report damage to named landmarks, government sites and cultural institutions to indicate severity and symbolic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited: Buckingham Palace (gatepost, chapel hit), Westminster Abbey window damaged, South Africa House and law courts in the Strand damaged, St. Paul’s Cathedral (unexploded bombs guarded). Naming landmarks helps convey scale and significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vivid sensory description to convey immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ descriptive, sensory language (sounds of guns, drone of motors, whistling bombs, flashes and fires) to create a vivid sense of the event for readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative phrases: “the drone of plane motors,” “some bombs fell, whistling,” “the roar of the planes then faded,” “brilliant pillar of flame.” Such detail enhances reader engagement while remaining reportorial.
